catalog_quote: Elnur & Compes 2026: 34: "In this study, we provide evidence for three underlying level tones (L, M, and H) which typically form tonal contours on the surface. The three tones are not equally distributed. While L and M occur in all positions, the H tone is restricted, and we analyze it as having only a grammatical function." -- Elnur & Compes 2026: 52: "Since as a general rule the H tone is excluded from the word-initial position, Beria has no H-tone-only forms underlyingly. Instead, the underlying occurrence of the H tone is at the right edge of the root or on the FM." -- Osman 2006 (preprint pp. 15-16): "Zaghawa language manipulates tone grammatically to draw distinctions between singular and plural nouns and lexically to differentiate between varied meanings of the same word. This indicates that pitch is phonemic. Various levels of pitch and tone phonemes go together with consonants and vowels to make up syllables and words. ... The following tone features can be identified in Zaghawa: high [/], low [\], mid [─], falling [∧] and rising [∨].Contour tones may occur on short vowels."

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated by any opened source. Beria is described as a tone language with lexical and grammatical tone: three underlying level tones L, M, H (H restricted to the right edge of the root or the verbal final morpheme, i.e. grammatical) per Elnur & Compes 2026; five surface tones (H, M, L, falling, rising) per Osman 2006. Neither work, nor Compes 2021, Laureck 2024 or Wolfe & Adam 2018, uses the words stress or accent for the language itself. The only 'stress' mentions are orthographic: the Beria Giray Erfe script proposal (Priest 2008, SIL, L2/08-265, section E.2) lists 'U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE represents stress', and the SIL font page says 'Tone and stress marks are mutually exclusive. Tone markings occur in transcriptions, and stress markings occur in the writing system.' This shows the community orthography has a stress mark but gives no placement rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Elnur & Compes 2026: 52 note the H tone is excluded from word-initial position except in one alternative form of monosyllabic MH roots, and quote Yip (2002: 83) that H tone 'is often attracted to prominent positions (beginnings of things, edges, accented or stressed syllables)' -- a general remark, not a claim about Beria stress. Elnur & Compes 2026: 56 contrast Beria with Dazaga, whose two-tone system 'even shows restricted patterns comparable to a pitch accent system' (Walters 2016).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described at word level (verb forms and nouns) with grammatical tone marking number, TAM and polarity; Laureck 2024: 101 says plurality 'is generally associated with a change of the tonal pattern of the whole phrase or verb form'. Nothing is said about stress at any domain.
new_statements.identity_note: Osman 2006 and all the Cologne-group papers (Compes 2021, Laureck 2024, Elnur & Compes 2026) describe the Wagi/Wegi dialect of Sudan; Jakobi & Crass 2004, Crass & Jakobi 2000 and Khidir 1984 describe the Kube dialect of Chad. Glottolog has no separate dialect codes listed in the target record; all fall under zagh1240.

sources.note: Nothing about stress in Beria; 3 underlying level tones L/M/H, H grammatical and right-edge-restricted; 'accented or stressed syllables' appears only inside a Yip 2002 quotation (p. 52); Dazaga (not Beria) called 'comparable to a pitch accent system' (p. 56). Reports Jakobi & Crass 2004: 32-33, 61-64 as the grammar's tone pages and Wolfe 2001: 105-106 as proposing a basically binary tone opposition.
